utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Matthew Olmsted, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Appearing for Stanisic Defence, Zecevic and Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, Eric Tully, and Harriet Taylor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have Mr. Djekanovic back on the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to transcript, Ms. Harriet Taylor, T like tango. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, sir, good morning to you. I remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djekanovic. We left off -- we stopped yesterday for procedural reasons before we finished, so now we'll try very briefly to go through a few points that remain unclear after yesterday's examination, and I'll try to conclude as soon as possible. The same caution as yesterday, please speak more slowly for the interpreters. I understand your nervousness and your desire to explain all these events, but please mind the speed. I noticed in the transcript yesterday that perhaps because of overlapping between us some things remained unclear. When you spoke about that lunch, which you went to attend, you went practically because Pejic told you the command was there; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pejic suggested we go up there because he heard that they were gathering there for some sort of social occasion, and I took his advice, and Pejic and I went together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day or perhaps the day before that attack happened with the initial military success and then failure, and at that point none of the military commanders from the municipality were in town, nobody who could deal with the problem and that's why you went there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you went practically to see Peulic, who was the absolute commander on the entire territory of Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went to see Peulic but we knew that the others were there too -- I mean, I had been told that the others were there, the others in charge of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time Peulic as the officer leading military operations was the absolute commander in that region, there was a war going on?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the absolute commander. I don't know if his force was called tactical group, but I knew that the municipal brigade had its own commander. But still they were in effect subordinated to him. He commanded all the military operations, he made all the decisions, and led all the military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in a certain way, because you were under the immediate threat of war, he also had a decisive influence on you in view of the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't say that he had decisive influence on us as civilian authorities in areas of our competence. You couldn't say that he ordered us about or commanded our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking now about military activities, combat operations, control of territory in the area of combat operations. And in that sense, when you say that he was the absolute commander it's in that sense that I meant it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to the extent that we had any jurisdiction ourselves in military things. You know that we did not have any competence in military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You even mentioned that as far as combat operations are concerned when you heard that there was an action planned to take place in town, you had only been informed that the action had taken place?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. That happened often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in this specific case concerning this attack, that was one of the complaints you made during that picnic, if I can call it that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it demonstrated the complete lack of coordination of these military operations, overlapping between units, all these things that created problems for our men, for the army. And it was our good intention and suggestion that this kind of conduct should be redressed. Whether he really took note or appreciated what we said is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, you gave an interview to the Prosecution twice, in 2003 and now in March 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On both occasions it was a suspect interview?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on both occasions I was designated as a suspect and summoned as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The latest interview in Sarajevo you gave in the presence of an investigator, an interpreter, a Prosecutor. Did you have the impression that you were under pressure? Were you anxious about your status and possible criminal proceedings that could ensue in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end I signed my statement and agreed to state that I gave it voluntarily, which is true; but it's also true that I gave that statement as a suspect, that I had been summoned as a suspect, and that is not contested. And that certainly had an effect and has an effect on my evidence and very frequently my inability to explain the problem the way it occurred. You have to say yes or no to many questions rather than explain how it really was. Of course somebody qualified can build the whole picture out of that, but I was not always able to say all I know about a certain event. Very often I had to say just yes or no. I was very often interrupted, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were asked leading questions and you were asked to reply briefly and draw certain conclusions; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really would not like and will not comment here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And precisely because of this method and your status, you did not want to appear voluntarily as a Prosecution witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not want to be -- to appear voluntarily as a Prosecution witness. Even before when I was invited by some other parties to give statements, I did not agree. I refrained from all of that. And I had been invited both in the Brdjanin case and in the Krajisnik case, but by the Defence, not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I was able to see, in your interview there are many incomplete answers, many assumptions voiced. You couldn't remember always the dates, the event itself, all the details?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. If you analyse my evidence over the past days, you can certainly find dates that I had confused, the sequence of things confused. But I have to say again, after 17 years elapsed and under the circumstances under which I live, it's very difficult. I did not have the will or the strength or the time to be honest to gather all the information and to put things in chronological order. Whatever I had in terms of documents I gave to the Prosecution, but I had no time to dedicate to some sort of personal project to gather more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you never got a transcript from this latest interview, March 2009?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was videotaped, so I received the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you listened to that tape after you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Not before I travelled, but here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I just consult my client for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, Your Honour, just for the record and it should be corrected transcripts from 7th of October -- sorry, 7th, I think -- anyhow, page 1068, line 24, 25, this witness said that Zupljanin was the chief of Crisis Staff, but probably he meant that it was a context of question of my learned friend Ms. Korner that he was a chief of CSB. Just to correct it or maybe I can clarify with the witness if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, Your Honour, I don't need the mike then -- I'm just asking what line -- I've got page 1068 open. Where do you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 24, 25. Maybe it's 1069, sorry, it's my mistake. 24, 25. Sorry. I'll correct it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which day was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've seen it, Your Honour, it's 1069, lines 8 and 9. It says: "Zupljanin was head of the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, on which day?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can I clarify that with the witness or it's already fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djekanovic, just to remove one remaining unclarity. At the beginning when you were talking about the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region Krajina, it remained on the record that Stojan Zupljanin was at the head of that staff. In fact --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. He was never the head of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Brdjanin was at the head of the Crisis Staff for a while. I think you say so?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djekanovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I begin my re-examination, in the light of all the questions that were asked about the interview and the suggestions that were made to the witness about the leading questions and the like, may I formally now apply to have both interviews exhibited so that Your Honours can look at the context of all questions and answers. I think there are about a dozen or so questions. So it's the interview of the 25th of March, which will be 65 ter 10119 and the interview of the 12th of March -- sorry, 12th of June, 2003, 10118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you have something to say about that application?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is opposed to the admission of these documents. First of all, they're not on the 65 ter list, which means that in keeping with the instruction given by the Trial Chamber and the decision of the Trial Chamber they cannot be exhibited. Second, using a suspect interview in the form of interview not in the form of statement, unlike other witness statements, would be inappropriate unless the Prosecution intends to impeach this witness and treat him as a hostile witness. Since this is not the case here, I believe it would be inappropriate to use a suspect interview. And when I met with the witness, he did impart to me his impression that he was under pressure and that frequently in that interview he was giving some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you there, Mr. Krgovic. You can't give evidence, but having regard to your basic objection haven't you made it an issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I didn't show the witness his interview, for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but by your questions you've made it an issue, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but only on leading questions and that was confirmed by the witness. That was his impression of the way the interview led. If the Prosecution claims there were no leading questions, I have no problem with that. I just asked the witness about his impression without quoting from the interview. He just confirmed. So if the Prosecution wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you said the witness confirmed. Didn't he say: I won't comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that questions were put to him in such a way that he had to answer yes or no, which means that that's the way questions were formulated. He does not know the term "leading question" or what it means. He was frequently interrupted during the interview. He was not allowed to finish his explanations or state his position on certain issues, but right now during his evidence he did explain his position on many things and that is his evidence. Now, exhibiting the interview with a view to impeaching or discrediting this witness I don't think is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not actually seeking to impeach the witness. I am seeking to have this made an exhibit because of the large --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, before you reply, I think Mr. Zecevic also had something to say on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Stanisic is also opposed. Among other things, I believe that it is completely inadmissible after the completion of a cross-examination for the Prosecution to tender new documents. Essentially that would mean that we have to go back to examination with these new documents and then finish cross-examining the witness. I don't think that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The answer is there's no right to re-cross-examine unless leave is sought. The simple issue is this: Mr. Krgovic in his cross-examination raised with the witness the way he alleges the interview has been conducted and he indeed went -- said even more in his argument why it shouldn't go in. It is, therefore, only right and proper, and I'm afraid that's the result of cross-examination like that, that Your Honours have a chance to look at the interview, see how it went, what was said, and what the form of the questions were. And I'm afraid that's what results when cross-examination is conducted in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, this matter is more simply resolved than counsel on either side appear to understand it to be, for the simple reason that when the suggestions were put to the witness by Mr. Krgovic the witness at the end of it all says that it's something on which he would not comment. So, therefore, there is no evidence - and I underline the word "evidence" in that regard - and the Chamber will simply disregard that whole exchange between the witness and counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I -- at one point he said I'm not prepared to comment, but he was agreeing with all the other suggestions that were being made about the interview. In your interview there are incomplete answers, many assumptions voiced, you couldn't remember the dates, the event, or the details. That's true. And then further down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in our view that does not constitute any wrong techniques for interview on the part of the Prosecution. I mean, the only thing we have is an allegation made by counsel Krgovic that it was all very leading. And as far as we understand the witness's answers, he wouldn't want to comment on whether he thought they were leading or not. And that's the end of the story, and hence our decision to simply disregard the allegation made by Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You -- let's deal with your interview, Mr. Djekanovic, because I am going to ask you about parts of it. On the first occasion you were interviewed on tape, and you were given a copy of the tape. Is that right? Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did receive a copy of the recording on the tapes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because there were two interviews and interview in Hague just for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I said on the first occasion, in 2003, you had -- I didn't say "interview in The Hague" - you were given a copy of the tape?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was given a copy of the tape immediately. I was given six or seven audio-cassettes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed you had your own transcript prepared, or you prepared your own transcript of what was said in that interview?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I needed quite some time to listen to it slowly and to type the text out myself and to -- well, it's a question of how acceptable it is as evidence, but it is true that I did transcribe parts of it that were written in Serbian. I didn't type the bits that were in English, but everything that was in Serbian I did type out for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you've told the Court, you on the second occasion the whole interview was videotaped, and you were given a copy of the videotape immediately on the conclusion of that interview. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already confirmed that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were also told on both occasions, weren't you, that if you wanted a lawyer present you could have a lawyer present?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. In the first interview or during the first interview I didn't know that I had the right to an attorney. This was given -- told to me at the beginning of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And were you told that the choice was yours. "Q. Do you wish to have a lawyer present for this interview?" And you said: "Right now in this phase of the proceedings, I don't see that I can change anything." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is absolutely correct that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And on the second occasion do you agree that you had definitely been told in advance you had the right to have a lawyer present?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though the interview was conducted fairly recently, I received a summons saying -- or that I was being questioned as a suspect and that I was being interviewed in relation to the Zupljanin/Stanisic case. This is what it said on the summons that I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it tell you that you had the right to have a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute that it was perhaps said even though this interview took place fairly recently, a couple of months ago, I'm not -- I'm not disputing that even though I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to now go back over some of the matters you've been asked about in cross-examination first of all by Mr. Zecevic. You were asked about the community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you identified the municipalities that you said belonged to that community, including that of Jajce. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jajce in fact made an application, did it not, to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that detail. Perhaps the Municipal Assembly of Jajce had submitted such a request. I'm not talking about the municipality of Jajce as part of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I do not dispute that the Serbian municipality of Jajce, including the municipality of Jezero, which is now part of the Republika Srpska area did that. But not the entire municipality of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'll just show you a document, which I'm not going to ask to exhibit - it's purely to refresh your memory. Could you have a look, please, at -- what did you say the number was? 65 ter 10129. That's a document headed: "The Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Jajce," dated the 22nd of February, 1992, so some three -- two weeks after your municipality had applied to join. Request for admission into the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And then if we go down the document in English, please, the following delegates were elected to the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly. And did you know those gentlemen who are named there, Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew the first person, and I stand by what I first said that this was the Serbian municipality of Jajce and not the entire region of the municipality of Jajce. I know Dragan Milicic, I knew him then. I still know him today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say, I'm not disputing that it was claimed by Herceg-Bosna as well. I'm merely pointing out that it also had links apparently with the Autonomous Region of Krajina. All right, that's all I ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honours, that was simply to remind the witness, so I don't want it exhibited or even marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next I want to turn to the question of communications, please, and what you said to Mr. Zecevic yesterday. And this is the transcript at page 1426. It was put to you by Mr. Zecevic that telephone lines were also cut off, right, and you said: "The greatest part of that period, no telephone communications were available at all. Only later did we establish one telephone line through the post office in Banja Luka, but that was much later. In those first days we had no telephones at all. "Q. You mean to say there was one telephone line -- first of all, at the beginning there was no communication with the outside world, and then later one telephone line was established for the whole of the municipality; correct? "A. Yes, I'm talking about the whole of the municipality. "Q. So your only means of communication, apart from your physical ability or inability to leave the municipality and then only to Banja Luka, was this one telephone that was made to work? "A. Yes, in that period, yes." And you confirmed the next page that was -- that in June and July you had no power, no telephone communication, and the fact that there was no electricity, et cetera. Do you want to think about that for a moment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking of. I know what was going on at the time. I talked about the civilian telephone lines, and I didn't speak about the military or the police lines. I don't know about that and don't wish to talk about that, but as for the fact that there were electricity shortages, telephone lines were cut off, we had to dismantle fuel pump in the Proleks plant in order to provide some kind of mechanism to be able to pump water. These are the difficulties that we were encountering, but I don't really wish to speak about that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I am only interested in the phones. Do you stick by your answer, that in the whole of June and July there was no telephone communication?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say whether it was throughout the whole of June until that conflict broke out on the 11th. There were conflicts over those days and weeks, and they were gaining in intensity in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The problem with the electricity supplies were a broader problem, not only a problem of the Kotor Varos municipality. The Kotor Varos municipality did have specific problems at the time -- a specific problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you have another look, please, at document P87. Okay. Crisis Staff meeting 7th of July. Can we move across the page to the English, please. Item 2: Under this item all Crisis Staff members reported one by one on their activities in the course of a day. The planned harvest programme in Kotor Varos municipality was upheld. Reconnection of telephones for the needs of the public auditing services for Kotor Varos was authorised. So, Mr. Djekanovic, you had a telephone line, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was one telephone line that was provided, some kind of technical re-connection was done. We didn't go into how this was done in order to make it possible for the public auditing service to work. Some phones were put into service. Later I know that telephone lines were established again for some specific institutions. I don't know exactly technically how this was done. All I know is that there was one single telephone connection between Kotor Varos and Banja Luka, and we proceeded on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says "authorised." Was it the fact that you were controlling the use of the telephones, not that they weren't available or the telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not controlling or were able to control this, but there were requests to enable lines to function by making switches at the post office switchboard so that they could work. We did not have an unlimited number of telephone lines at our disposal, and we did not authorise who should have telephone lines or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm not going to pursue this matter any further either. You've said to I believe it was Mr. Zecevic yesterday - I'll just check that, it may be Mr. Krgovic - yes, it was Mr. Krgovic, this. You were dealing with the -- what you describe as the people coming into town as refugees, and you said this: "In any case, nowhere were civilians removed by force." Again, is that an answer that you want to confirm -- sorry, I should say it's page 1457. Mr. Djekanovic, is that the evidence that you want the Court to understand is right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the population being removed from their homes by force and that they were forced to evacuate, I do stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're saying at no stage in the whole of the conflict in Kotor Varos was there ever a time when people were driven out of their homes in villages and put into camps - is that what you're saying? - and prisons?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individual people being arrested or detained, but as for entire families to be removed by force from their homes or entire families being arrested, I definitely say that nothing like that happened. A good part of the population came of their own initiative, asking us to place them under protection briefly. But this didn't last that long, and they asked for transports to be organised for them to be able to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to -- that's what you want the Court to understand is your evidence about the events. All right. Next, you were asked yesterday by -- this was by Mr. Zecevic about the Crisis Staff, and this is page 1411. And the question was: "When the Crisis Staff was formed, it became the sole authority in the municipality, uncontested power; is that correct? "A. Yes. "Q. When I say 'uncontested,' what I mean by that is that all the rights and duties for normal life in the municipality, the economy, the utilities, the schools rested with the Crisis Staff? "A. Yes, all matters except for military matters. "Q. In that sense you absolutely didn't require any instructions because the legal powers in that sense and the text of the law are very clear in terms of what are your powers, responsibilities, rights; is that right? "A. Yes." I want to understand, and I think the Trial Chamber need to understand, Mr. Djekanovic, what you're saying about that in respect of the police. Is that answer intended to include the fact that you had authority over the police in the sense of giving them instructions or orders?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself wanted to ask for an opportunity to respond to this question. It partially referred to the Crisis Staff decision to introduce a curfew in the municipality. These are all dates after the 11th of June. Up until the 11th of June there was several Crisis Staff. Each of the ethnic groups had their own Crisis Staff who were acting within that segment of the population. The Crisis Staff that I was at the head of didn't exist at that time. After the 11th of June it was entrusted with the entire civilian power in the municipality of Kotor Varos. When I say "civilian powers," it means that we did have the right to provide logistic supplies for the military, to secure fuel. Often we had to find ways to collect money, also to buy ammunition. I do not dispute that we did that. As for the use of units, I do not dispute that it was in the part of the powers of the municipality to deal with such decisions because they were problems that we were facing in the Crisis Staff, but the Crisis Staff could not decide on the use of police units or military units. We -- the Crisis Staff that I was heading did not have nor is there any evidence that they had the power to order any use of the units. We did suggest very often, and the suggestions would refer to such matters like that it was necessary to provide security for populations of a certain area. The example is the village of Garici, which was a joint suggestion of the Crisis Staff to secure additional forces to secure that village, and that is where we met with the support of the military and the police. But again, we did not decide when some military action would take place, how it would take place. We did not have such powers. I state that with full responsibility, nor is there any evidence that as the Crisis Staff we were able to do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but I think -- I'm not thinking, I'm sure, that the witness stated that Crisis Staff imposed curfew in the municipality and that was a part of his -- I mean, its authority. So I should -- I think that my learned friend should ask him again for the correction in transcript or maybe our witness can confirm that. He mentioned during his answer but it was not put in the transcript you -- to the main issue that Mr. Djekanovic is speaking very fast and that certain portion of his statement cannot go into the record. And I kindly ask Mr. Djekanovic to please slow down for a half of speed so that we have everything precise in the transcript. But this particular part where he said that Crisis Staff imposed curfew and that he was authorised -- and that Crisis Staff was authorised for that is -- it isn't a part of particular transcript, which is quite important issue, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Isn't it at page 18, line 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a beginning of his answer, but later on, it should be around line 19 or 20, he expanded his response in regard to police authorities' curfew. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've raised over and over again now what I say is an improper way of giving the witness the answer. If it is thought that something else was said, then the witness can be asked to repeat what he said and not given the answer in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we go back to the question I actually asked, Mr. Djekanovic, which was this: When you said what you said about the powers of the Crisis Staff - and can we simply concentrate on the police, forget about the military - were you saying that you could give orders to the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we could not issue orders to the police and there are such minutes from Crisis Staff meetings. They were shown here as well, where it is clearly stated that the Crisis Staff is not authorised to interfere in the jurisdiction of the police. There are such minutes of meetings here and they were shown here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I just want -- so that everybody's clear about what you are saying. So in relation to the document that you were shown about the curfew, you say that the powers of the Crisis Staff included imposing a curfew and the police obviously would have to carry it out. If the police, for whatever mad reason, had refused to carry it out, would you have had the authority to order them to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I understand -- I don't understand the question sufficiently. We didn't have the need for something like that. The member of the police was a member of the joint Crisis Staff, so we reached our decisions together. At different points in time different organs make decisions relating to the crisis situation or the Crisis Staff. We were in a situation of imminent danger of war, and the situation which was such that war was already being waged in the municipality -- in the whole area of Bosnia-Herzegovina war was waging -- war was being waged --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Okay. I think you explained earlier, but the point of a Crisis Staff, having the police and a representative of the military attend, was to coordinate activities. Is that right? I think you said that earlier on. Is that right, Mr. Djekanovic? A simple yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Crisis Staff were people in certain positions in the executive arm of authorities in Kotor Varos. Among them was the chief of police and of course naturally it was the task of the Crisis Staff to coordinate, to interlink, organise, and assume responsibility for the civilian life in the territory of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I think we've covered that and you've explained your position. I want to deal now with the special police as such. And can we understand what your evidence is now about the special police. First, did you ask for assistance from Banja Luka to take power on the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we asked for assistance from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From whom was that assistance sought?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knocked on every door, the corps command, the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did Stojan Zupljanin, as head of the police, the CSB, supply you with assistance?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question at all. I don't know if he supplied us with assistance, but as help to the -- to our police one unit from the Banja Luka police was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. May -- can you ask him again to repeat the answer because it is not precise in transcript, line -- it's page 22, line 4. I don't give any details, so you can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, Mr. Djekanovic. Did Stojan Zupljanin, as head of the police, the CSB, supply you with assistance? Could you tell us again what your answer is.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The competent authorities of the police in Banja Luka sent one unit to assist Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But witness -- witness said first army and then police, so please ask him to confirm or not to confirm what he was -- said. We have -- we have audio -- audio file here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you mention that the army sent assistance?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said we knocked on every door. We addressed the army, the corps, and the police for assistance, and I'm saying this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm asking you -- in fact, you did say that earlier and it's been recorded. But I'm asking you now about whether the police sent assistance and you said twice: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He said simply and clearly: CSB sended [sic] a police in assistance to military unit, in assistance to military unit, and to the police then. That was his real answer, but okay, I will clarify that with the audio files. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've asked you twice now and you've given the same answer twice, Mr. Djekanovic, but I'm going to ask you for the third time: Did the Banja Luka CSB in accordance with your request for assistance send you a unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Banja Luka centre of security services did send a unit, but I have to add - and it's very difficult for me as a man who's between a rock and a hard place, I'm aware of this - it's equally clear that others sent help too to units, and there was a headquarters of this action. The main commander, the chief commander, of all combat and military operations in Kotor Varos was Commander Peulic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Who -- I'm sorry, have you ever said this before to anybody?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is whether anyone ever asked me. No one ever put a question to me about who was the commander of military operations, who commanded the armed units in the municipality of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We are talking about the special police, Mr. Djekanovic, and I want to understand what your evidence is at the end of this. Are you saying that a unit known as the special police was sent from Banja Luka or not? It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the umpteenth time I'm answering Your Honours within three, four minutes. A unit from Banja Luka was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which format, which size, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Was that unit known as the special police unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that question you can answer this way or that way. In my interviews you did not allow me to explain this. Yesterday in my evidence I said in that unit, for all I know, there were some people - and I gave a few names and I thought over now it - there were some people who had never been in the police, I'm talking about that unit that arrived in Kotor Varos. I mentioned Slobodan Dubocanin, who I believed to be the head of that unit. I know that he had never been in the police before, and there was also his relative, a military volunteer who had participated in the war in Slovenia, Damir Dubocanin, who also for all I know had never been in the police. There were also some other people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I wonder is that the criterion? You told us at the beginning of I think yesterday that Savo Tepic when he was appointed head of the police in your municipality was never in the police before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that post of the commander of the police is a case in point. That happened often. I don't know if that is reason, but for someone to be admitted into the police without first undergoing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you said that doesn't prevent you to be in a police unit at a certain moment, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible. I'm not challenging that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've referred to your interview and you said we wouldn't let you explain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've referred to your interview and you said we wouldn't let you explain, so I'm going to take you through the parts, please. First interview in May -- I'm sorry, 12th of June, 2003, page 69 on the screen, please. Oh, it's 10118.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we have decision that this interview can be used, if I understand your decision correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, the decision was I couldn't make it an exhibit in this case. I'm perfectly entitled now that he has raised the matter to go through it with him, and I'm going to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm afraid that my -- okay, it's page 70. Is it on the screen? Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The context is there's been a break, and I may say on the page before it's said to you: "If at any stage you feel you're too tired to go on answering questions please let us know straight away." And the context was you were looking at the Crisis Staff minutes of the 21st of June. And you said -- and I -- you were asked whether -- you'd reminded yourself before you came to the meeting, and you said -- right. "No, what I meant is that I understood these issues better because I was an active participant. But it's entirely possible that I do have a copy of these minutes ... we must say that when the undesired events did occur, people were driven away, houses were left empty and deserted. And then looting began. Destruction of property, destruction of items in the house. Especially the special unit of the police that was stationed there acted badly." And the investigator Mr. Dupas, who was interviewing you, said, We'll talk about the special unit in a moment, and it goes back to Brdjanin. Do you agree, because you've got a transcript of this yourself in your possession, Mr. Djekanovic, the first mention of the special police unit in this interview came from you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit, special police, that's what we called them, whatever name anyone chose to gave [as interpreted] them. I don't dispute that I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then on the next -- I'm not sure where the page is, page 71. Right. You asked about the special unit. "Did you know Ljuban Ecim?" And you said: "I met him for the first time a couple of days after he first arrived. I did not see him a lot, but I met him, yes." "Did you know Mr. Dubocanin?" And you said, yes, you knew him before. And then you were asked whether you knew he was a Crisis Staff -- a regional -- member of the regional Crisis Staff. "You say this special police unit was in Kotor Varos. Who had sent it to Kotor Varos? "That was part of the activities that had to be put under some kind of control, so this came I assume was ... co-ordinated from Banja Luka, it was not under initiative. "Do you mean it was sent from Banja Luka without any consultation with you or your Crisis Staff? "I'm not saying nobody asked us or consulted us, but we could not decide who was going to participate in the units, in the take-over. There was a need for the Banja Luka security services centre to become involved" -- sorry, it's the next page, is it? And then can we go to the page after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 74 I'm told. Your Honour, I have no idea why the hard copy and the thing in the e-court are different page numbers. No, no. Page 72. Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 72: "Q. Did you ask the Crisis Staff and the CSB in Banja Luka to provide you with extra police manpower for the purposes of the take-over? "A. We did ask for assistance to preserve control over everything, to prevent others from taking control. "Q. Is what you're telling us in relation to this Crisis Staff meeting" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "the men who got out of control? "A. The special unit of police, yes. That's clear. I mean, you could see in many of the minutes of the Crisis Staff, I asked for it, many of the other members asked for it. It was a problem we needed to solve because the assistance we had originally asked for just ended up giving us a headache ..." And as I say, there are endless other references to the special police unit, Mr. Djekanovic, in this interview and the next. Can we have your final answer, please. Are you saying this special unit was a special police unit sent by Banja Luka, who then -- well, that's the first question. Is that what your evidence is or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- Mr. Djekanovic, sorry, the interpreters didn't catch your answer, so, please, would you repeat your answer. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was that a unit was sent from Banja Luka, and I'm asserting here that we requested that assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the unit, the special unit, a special unit of the police as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could fall into a deep confusion if I tried to pretend that I know how the unit was formed, what were its origins, and what was its size. I know that it arrived, that the centre of the security services was involved, and I know that in the territory of Kotor Varos all military units are now aside, were under the command of Mr. Peulic. He was the Commander-in-Chief of all these units -- in fact, every unit of course had its own commander, its own command. But the commander of all military operations in the municipality of Kotor Varos was Mr. Peulic, who was the commander of one of those military units, the biggest, the best-equipped unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, I don't -- I'm not asking you how the unit was formed, what its origins were, or what its size was. Was there a special unit from the Banja Luka CSB under the authority of Mr. Dubocanin who was reporting to you at the Crisis Staff meetings? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You now sort of expanded the question, whether it was under the command of Dubocanin and whether it was responsible to us. I cannot answer in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not -- all right, one more time and then I will leave it, Mr. Djekanovic. Was there a unit of the special police operating in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody called it that, special police unit, and I have no reason to call it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have looked at - and I'm not going to ask you to look at it again - endless Crisis Staff meetings dealing with the problems that were being caused by the special police. Was it that group that was -- the complaints were being made about and that Mr. Dubocanin told you was going to leave Kotor Varos at the beginning of July?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my statement you can conclude that it is the way you put it because I did not have the opportunity to explain in full all of the problems that surrounded this matter. We spoke a lot in the past few days about those undesirable things and the people within that unit who were out of control, not by the Crisis Staff but they were out of the control of their own commands, and they did all sorts of things. I never contested that. And the Crisis Staff certainly did demand that such conduct by one part of the personnel be put an end to. But not all of the unit was like that, nor is it true that the whole unit was out of control or that the whole unit, as you would like to have it, did these things. Yes, individuals did, and we opposed it clearly in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, Your Honours, I know it's time for the break but in light of the answer "from my statement you conclude it's the way you put it because I did not have the opportunity to explain in full all of the problems," I'm renewing my application to make these documents exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, you asked again for the earlier statements of Mr. Djekanovic to be admitted into evidence. Let me give you the result first and then the reasons afterwards. The result is negative. We will not allow it to be admitted into evidence. The reasons are the following: First of all, this interview was given by the witness when he was a suspect, and that is the main reason why we think that it would be ill-advised to allow it to be admitted into evidence. There are too many caveats that surround a statement that has been given by someone who was a suspect that it would be safe for the Chamber to admit such statements into evidence. Secondly, we understand that the reasons why you now apply for the statement to be admitted was different from the reasons why you applied the first time because the first application was made, as we understood it, as an attempt to counter counsel Krgovic's allegations that the statement had been given under pressure. And for the reasons that we explained, we simply disregarded that allegation. Now the second time was for the purpose of supplementing his oral testimony in court with the written material information that he gave about the identity of the special police unit and the actions in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. That's not right, Your Honour. I accept the decision Your Honours have made, but just for the record, I applied because he said: You didn't give me an opportunity to answer. That's the reason I applied. I repeated my application. Not because of a supplement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case, that just fortifies our decision, namely, that we ruled on that matter once, and we're not going to reconsider it. We thought that your second application was actually founded in something different, namely, for the purpose of clarifying the material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, let -- I mean, let's not go into a discussion. The ruling is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The third reason why we thought it would be unwise is that if we were to allow the statement to come in as such in toto the entire statement, then we would probably have to allow the Defence counsels to bring up certain other aspects. Now the Defence counsels have had the chance to put all the questions to the witness relating to his earlier statements because they've had the statements in advance and they've had the chance to read it and they could have used it in cross-examination, but I suppose that the questions that the counsels did ask in relation to his statements were asked under the premise or under the condition that these statements would not be admitted into evidence. And if now we admit them, we think it would be only fair to the Defence counsels to actually give them a chance to review any questions that they might wish to put. So in order to simply avoid the issue of re-opening the cross-examination, we add that third argument to our decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours -- I understand, and I accept the decision that you've made. Can I just say this: It is almost axiomatic so that for the future we don't have the situation arising again, that if suggestions are made about the way in which an interview is conducted, either by counsel or by the witness himself, well, then it is only fair that Your Honours should be able to see how the interview went. So if these suggestions are being made again, I will be renewing this application. It's axiomatic in the jurisdiction of which I come from and I think Judge Hall comes from that if counsel ask questions and a lot of questions or make suggestions about a document, the document is made part of the evidence. As I say, I accept your ruling on this occasion. The second thing is that I don't know whether Your Honours are aware that a witness who is treated as a suspect has rights which are not given to other people who are interviewed, one is the presence of a lawyer and one is the right not to answer questions. Those are read to him in each and every occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are fully aware of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't take up any more time in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And let me just, since you raised it yourself, remind both counsels as counsel from both sides, that of course the legal system that applies before this Tribunal is not a common law nor civil law. It is a hybrid, and it is a system that applies and develops on its own premises and its own terms. So you cannot always rely exclusively on answers provided in one or the other legal system because here we have to do things differently. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, you are just reading my thoughts. That was the -- thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue relating to the material evidence which we perhaps erroneously thought was behind your second application, we intended to address that issue by allowing you, if you wish, to confront the witness with whatever other parts of his earlier statements that have to do with the issue of the special police unit. Because it is obvious that this issue is crucial to the evidence of -- given by this witness. And so what we will do you -- will allow you to do once we have ruled that the statements are inadmissible is to allow you to put up to the witness further parts of his statements which supplements or maybe even contradicts his oral testimony in court. And for the record, I don't think that any doubt should be left about the priority of evidence given. It applies to both legal systems, both the common law and the civil law, that's evidence given under oath directly and orally before the Court prevails over written statements and written evidence not given under oath. So in both legal systems no doubt remains that in the end it is the spoken word in the court in front of the Judges that will prevail. Now, if this information is supplemented in one way or the other by earlier statements made by the witness, then of course that goes into the final basis on which we will assess the probative value of the witness's testimony. So, Mrs. Korner, you will have another chance to put to the witness a couple of other parts if you wish; but otherwise, that's as far as we will go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, I'm going to move on because I'm anxious that Mr. Olmsted gets the chance to call the next witness. Your Honours have in any event the transcript of the earlier evidence he gave about the special police, and I don't think there's much point in taking it any further. So, Your Honours, I've just got one short topic further to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Usher, will you bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I just want finally to ask you about the meetings or meeting you had with Stojan Zupljanin. When you were testifying about this on the 8th of October at page 1108 you had been asked about one of the meetings of the Crisis Staff, and you were asked this: "You had a meeting, did you, with Mr. Zupljanin? "I don't recall details whether on the following day I held or there was held. I did have a couple of meetings with Zupljanin. They were not overall official meetings. You can see from the report that we'd entrusted the head of the police station, but I don't recall that on the following day a meeting with Stojan Zupljanin was held." And this was -- perhaps I better give the exhibit number of this meeting you're referring to. I'll just find it. P81 it was. "Will you did, however, have a meeting, didn't you, with Stojan Zupljanin and you said more than one meeting but after these killings? "After those killings, I did have meetings with Stojan Zupljanin. How many times, when, what the dates were I don't remember but there weren't many such meetings. "All right. What were you saying to Stojan Zupljanin at these meetings? "I conveyed to him the positions of the Crisis Staff about our remarks and information, about the conduct of individuals as part of the special unit. "What did you want him to do? "We wanted him for the unit to be organisationally and structural constantly under control, that it should not relax and it should not be permitted for individuals to wilfully do the things that we had referred to earlier. In any case" -- oh, sorry. "And how many meetings, and what was his response to that? "In any case the event was" - this is your answer - "that he would do everything that was in his power to prevent these people behaving in the way that they did. "Who did this? Who was in command of the special unit? "At the beginning of yesterday's hearing I said I don't know exactly who it was. According to my information it was Slobodan Dubocanin." Now, yesterday and today you appear to be saying that you only had one meeting, an informal meeting at a picnic at which Stojan Zupljanin was present and all you did was talk in general terms about the military in particular, and you never addressed any specific complaint to Mr. Zupljanin. Which is right? What you said last Wednesday or what you said yesterday and earlier today?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say yesterday that the topic of the conversation with Stojan Zupljanin was just the military. I said that the topic were co-ordination and the functioning and the overlap of the authority or the powers, and I said that meeting was not only attended by Zupljanin but by Peulic and by some other commanders of the units. From what I remember this is what I said. I don't see that the first and second statements are that different. I did mention the conclusions of the Crisis Staff, but it's also true that the topic was much broader than what can be concluded from the answers during my first interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just finally on this topic have a look at the second interview at page 59, and it's 65 ter 1019 -- sorry, 10119. And could we go, please, to page 59 of 67. Yeah. In the middle of the page -- well, thank you very much. "All we are really trying to establish is this: At whatever meeting you had with Stojan Zupljanin, did you tell him that the behaviour of these murdering criminals had to be prevented?" The previous page it talks about the special police. "Yes. "And that effectively the members of the special unit had to be pulled out of Kotor Varos? "Very soon after that this happened." So is that right what you said in interview, you told him that the murdering -- the behaviour of these murdering criminals in the special unit had to be prevented?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals from the special police and the special unit, yes. This is what I said. That was the topic of discussion at many Crisis Staff meetings and you can see that in the minutes. I cannot dispute that here. I mean, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, thank you very much for attending. That concludes your testimony. You are now released as a witness. We appreciate your assistance, and we take note of your patience and the personal inconvenience that you would have experienced having regard to the breaks in your testimony. So you may now return home, and we wish you a safe trip. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry. We are ready to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, Your Honours, if our clients at certain stage will be in situation to address the Chamber about the issue that I raised yesterday on 65 ter Conference about the actual state and conditions of their health and, you know -- if you think that it's necessary to be informed. I mean, I'm not urging you now, maybe after this witness or whatever is convenient for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Will you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milenko Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 30th of March, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a notary now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever previously testify before this Tribunal in another procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I would first like to go over your legal background briefly. You started your legal career as a judge at the Sanski Most basic court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long were you a judge for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: For two years approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us what those two years were, what years?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: 1990, 1991, until late March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And kind of cases did you hear as a judge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Civilian matters -- civil matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from your position as a judge, what was the next position you held in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: After that I was appointed as public prosecutor in the basic public prosecutor's office in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when you were appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: It was towards the end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who formally appointed you to that position of basic prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: I received a letter of appointment signed by the then-president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long were you the basic prosecutor in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Until the 10th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after you left that position in Sanski Most, did you hold the position of deputy prosecutor in Banja Luka until 2004?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then after that position, between 2004 and 2008, were you working for the district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As you are the first prosecutor witness to testify in this case, I would like you to describe briefly the organisation of the prosecution service and the courts in the Republika Srpska from April 1992 throughout the rest of 1992. First of all, according to the laws of the Republika Srpska under which ministry of the government did the prosecutor's offices and courts fall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: The court prosecution offices were separate organs of the judiciary branch of Republika Srpska. They were organised at the basic level, the level of basic courts and basic prosecutor's offices for the region of the municipality. There were higher courts and higher prosecutor's offices, and they comprised several basic courts and prosecutor's offices. And then there was also the Supreme Court of Republika Srpska and the republican prosecutor 's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, and it is relevant to our case, but my question was in this 1992 time-period, there were the courts and there was the prosecution service. They fell within a ministry at the Republika Srpska level, and which ministry was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: These were organs of the judiciary and were under the authority of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Now we've just described the various levels of both the prosecution service and the court service so we won't cover that any further. I want to move on to what kinds of criminal offences did the basic courts have first-instant jurisdiction over?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: The basic courts were in charge of all the crimes somewhere in 1992. The law was changed and all the powers were transferred to the basic level, the basic courts and basic prosecutor's offices as far as criminal matters were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I would like to show you 65 ter Exhibit 2621. And I'd like you to take a look at the first decision. It's marked -- I think it's number 170. Do you recognise that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a title: "The Decision on Real Jurisdiction on Regular Courts in Criminal Cases."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And is this the decision that gave the basic courts and accordingly the basic prosecutors jurisdiction -- first-instance jurisdiction over all criminal offences in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what's written in Article 1 of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be marked and admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in 1992 what criminal codes applied to the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: At that time the criminal code of the former SFRY was in effect and the criminal code of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as far as substantive law is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which of those criminal codes applicable to the Republika Srpska in 1992 criminalised war crimes and crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Those criminal cases were governed by the former criminal code of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what -- we talked about the substantive criminal law. What criminal procedure code applied to the Republika Srpska as of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to take us through the procedures for investigating and prosecuting a criminal case that existed in the Republika Srpska during the April to December 1992 time-period, and in particular what were the roles of the police, the prosecutor, the courts in this process? Let me ask the question. First of all, how were criminal proceedings initiated? What had to happen first before a criminal case could begin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Most often the police would submit to the competent prosecutor's office a criminal report, a criminal complaint. In that criminal complaint information would be given about the person suspected of having committed a crime, with a brief description of the crime itself and the legal qualification of the act. And along with this criminal report evidence would be submitted, be it documentary evidence such as witness statements or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that mostly it was the police who submitted criminal reports to the prosecution office. Who else could submit criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: A criminal report could be filed by any physical or legal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But how often would that happen as far as the number of type of criminal reports where it was filed by someone other than the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Most often the police would file criminal reports. Perhaps 90 per cent of all criminal reports would be filed by the police. The remaining 10 per cent were filed by other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in the 10 per cent of cases where someone else filed a criminal report with the prosecution office, who verified the allegations in the criminal report? Who collected any additional evidence necessary to substantiate that criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: In those cases the competent prosecutor would ask the police to conduct vetting and run checks, collect evidence and any information that would be useful in conducting criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And prior to a police officer filing a criminal report with your office, what actions were the police supposed to take to investigate the case they were going to bring to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: The police. Depending really on what kind of case it was, the police collected material evidence such as documents, would take statements from witnesses who had the facts of the case. It was not unusual for investigative actions to be taken such as on-site investigation, and that on-site investigation would be handled by an investigative judge with a team of scene-of-crime officers, and a forensic technician, and the prosecutor would frequently attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, who was responsible -- who had the responsibility to identify and arrest perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, it was primarily the task of the police to detect perpetrators and collect evidence relevant to criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was it also the police who was responsible -- who were responsible for arresting perpetrators as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The police was duty-bound to arrest the perpetrator and bring him or her before the investigative judge if that was justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what means did the police have at their disposal to locate and arrest perpetrators during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: The police had the human resources and the equipment to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did they also have informants in the field that allowed them to identify perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Usually information is required about possible perpetrators, and the police staff member would get such information from so-called informers, people who cooperated with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if a prosecutor's office received a criminal report from the police that lacked sufficient evidence to proceed with the case, what could the prosecutor do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Usually the prosecutor would require additional evidence to be collected, evidence and information that he could use in starting and conducting criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to be clear for the record, the prosecutor would require additional evidence to be collected by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Usually the prosecutor would turn to the police, although he could get certain documents from legal persons as well such as businesses, in certain criminal cases in which they believe legal persons such as businesses would have the documents required.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, once the prosecutor's office has a sufficient criminal report and substantiating evidence, what is the next procedural step in the process?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: The next step would be for the prosecutor to submit a request for investigation, and the whole case file would be put before the investigative judge. And the prosecutor would request the investigative judge to conduct an investigation that would include certain investigative actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in order to conduct those investigative actions, what assistance would the investigative judge require from the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Usually investigative actions would include the questioning of the suspect and witnesses. For instance, if the suspect or a witness would fail to respond to the court summons, the court could ask the police to bring the person in by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could the investigative judge also use the police to conduct searches and seizures?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The investigative judge could also ask the police to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about assistance with forensic work, would that also be the responsibility of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the centre for public security, specifically in Banja Luka, there was a section for forensic expertise. They would provide forensic expertise in different cases, such as ballistic expertise of weapons or dactyloscopic expertise or different expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier on-site investigations. Are these types of investigations conducted typically before or after the criminal report is filed with the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC
utterances.text: Usually the on-site investigation would be conducted before, as soon as a report of an event came, for instance that a body was found or that a road accident had taken place. The police would inform the investigative judge and a prosecutor, and then the investigative judge together with the prosecutor and a crime inspector and a crime technician would come on site. And the investigation would be led by the judge. The purpose of that investigation would be to describe the incident as accurately as possible and to find clues such as casing of ammunition, something that could be subjected to forensic expertise and used as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
